description: Response Explorer pilot library: 24 authored challenges over the six-provider API Project library.

pathNotation.rules: Structural paths use [] for any array element. Concrete selections ($.items[2].name) are normalised by replacing every [n] with []. Keys may not contain '.', '[' or ']'.

find-data.label: Find the Data
find-data.skill: Locate one property by reading names, values, types and structure.

understand-structure.label: Understand the Structure
understand-structure.skill: Recognise containers, relationships and roles of nodes.

select-needs.label: Select What the App Needs
select-needs.skill: Decide which fields an application goal requires.

difficulties.beginner: Small response or documented subtree, one or two nesting levels, simple property selection, at most four needs.
difficulties.intermediate: Arrays of objects, nested properties, several plausible fields, selecting several useful properties.
difficulties.advanced: Related samples, nested collections, nullable or optional data, identifiers versus full objects, displayed data versus technical metadata.

locate-by-meaning.label: Locate by meaning
locate-by-meaning.description: Match a described need to the one property that holds it by reading names, values and data types.

disambiguate-same-name.label: Same name, different level
disambiguate-same-name.description: The same key appears at more than one level; the parent decides what it means.

polymorphic-branch.label: Mixed entries and branches
polymorphic-branch.description: Entries in one list, or one object's branches, are different kinds; find the branch that carries the needed data.

similar-metric-choice.label: Look-alike measurements
similar-metric-choice.description: Several sibling counters or measurements have similar names; choose by what each one actually tallies.

equivalent-paths.label: More than one valid path
equivalent-paths.description: Two or more properties carry the same information; recognise each as valid.

display-vs-raw.label: Display-ready vs raw
display-vs-raw.description: Choose between a raw machine value and a value already formatted for people.

optional-null-handling.label: Optional and null values
optional-null-handling.description: A property may be null or missing; interpret that as 'optional', and plan a fallback.

container-vs-element.label: Collection vs one item
container-vs-element.description: Tell the node that holds many items from one item and from response-level information.

scope-classification.label: What does this describe?
scope-classification.description: Sort nodes by what they describe: an item, the whole page, or the request itself.

nesting-chain.label: Parent-to-child chains
nesting-chain.description: Trace a branch from a container to the list or value inside it.

alternatives-group.label: Group of named options
alternatives-group.description: Recognise an object whose children are alternatives labeled by name, unlike an array of numbered entries.

ownership.label: Who owns this list?
ownership.description: Identical-looking lists at different levels belong to different parents; the position in the structure decides.

pagination-controls.label: Page-level controls
pagination-controls.description: Find the siblings of a collection that control paging, and tell them from per-item data.

cross-reference.label: Identifier references
cross-reference.description: Understand a property that stores another entry's identity value instead of containing it.

app-need-selection.label: What the app needs
app-need-selection.description: Map each part of an application goal to the properties it requires, separating necessary, optional and unneeded data.

invisible-need.label: Needed but never shown
invisible-need.description: Some data is never displayed but is required for a later step, such as an identifier used for a follow-up request.

wrapper-vs-content.label: Wrapper and content
wrapper-vs-content.description: Needs are spread across an entry that wraps an item and the item inside it; same-named properties have different owners.

conditional-need.label: A need that depends on a flag
conditional-need.description: One value is only meaningful together with a companion flag, so both are needed.

flag-vs-score.label: Yes/no flag or numeric score
flag-vs-score.description: The same concepts appear as flags, scores and metadata; choose the representation the application's decision uses, and nothing more.

misconceptions.auto-too-broad: Selected a container that holds the answer instead of the specific node.
misconceptions.auto-too-specific: Selected a detail inside the right container instead of the container the goal needs.
misconceptions.auto-sibling: Selected a neighbouring property that describes something different.
misconceptions.auto-unrelated: Selected a node from a branch unrelated to the goal.
misconceptions.auto-unneeded: Selected a property the stated goal does not need.
misconceptions.similar-metric: Chose a measurement with a similar name that counts something different.
misconceptions.wrong-kind-of-value: Chose a value of the wrong kind (for example text where a number was needed).
misconceptions.status-vs-payload: Confused information about the request (status, error group) with the data the app asked for.
misconceptions.technical-metadata: Chose technical or housekeeping data that the application never displays.
misconceptions.list-size-vs-item-metric: Chose a number that counts the items in a response instead of a number describing one item.
misconceptions.echo-vs-output: Chose data the response repeats from the request instead of data the service produced.
misconceptions.bookkeeping-vs-content: Chose a record of how the answer was produced instead of the answer.
misconceptions.legacy-field: Chose a field that is present but unused or always zero.
misconceptions.kind-of-other-thing: Chose a label that describes a different object than the one the goal is about.
misconceptions.raw-vs-display: Chose a raw value meant for calculation when a ready-to-display value was needed (or the reverse).
misconceptions.identifier-vs-label: Confused an identifier meant for programs with a label meant for people (or the reverse).
misconceptions.fallback-vs-primary: Chose the always-present backup property instead of the primary property that may be empty.
misconceptions.one-vs-many: Chose one element when the whole collection was needed.
misconceptions.page-vs-item: Chose information about the page or response when information about the items was needed.
misconceptions.one-vs-group: Chose one option when the group that holds all options was needed.
misconceptions.too-specific-fact: Chose one fact inside a group when the group itself was needed.
misconceptions.same-name-other-owner: Chose a property with the same or a similar name that belongs to a different parent.
misconceptions.group-vs-value: Chose the group that holds the value instead of the value itself.
misconceptions.scope-confusion: Misjudged what a node describes (the item versus the request).
misconceptions.ordering-vs-pointer: Chose a property that orders entries instead of one that points to another entry.
misconceptions.timestamp-lookalike: Chose a number that looks like a time but plays a different role.
misconceptions.plausible-detail: Chose a real, plausible property that the stated goal does not need.
misconceptions.score-vs-flag: Chose a numeric score where a yes/no flag was needed.
misconceptions.polymorphic-entry: Misjudged which entry of a mixed list carries the reply.

feedbackTemplates.tooBroad: That node contains the answer, but it also contains a lot more. Open it and look for the one thing the goal asks for.
feedbackTemplates.tooSpecific: That is a detail inside the right area. The goal asks for something bigger than this single value; step back up.
feedbackTemplates.sibling: You are in the right neighbourhood, but this property sits next to the answer and describes something different. Compare what each neighbour holds.
feedbackTemplates.unrelated: That part of the response describes something else. Re-read the application goal and look for the branch that matches it.
feedbackTemplates.slotEmpty: Select a node in the tree, then press this slot's button.
feedbackTemplates.slotDuplicate: You used this same node for another slot. Each slot needs its own node.
feedbackTemplates.classifyEmpty: Choose a category for this node.
feedbackTemplates.classifyWrong: Not quite. Compare what this node describes with what each category means.
feedbackTemplates.setMissingCount: Your selection covers part of what the app needs, but {{n}} need(s) are not covered yet.
feedbackTemplates.setMinimalExtras: This challenge asks for only what the app needs. At least one selected property is not needed.
feedbackTemplates.setContainer: You selected a whole group. The app needs specific values from inside it, so choose the individual properties.
feedbackTemplates.setUnneeded: The app does not need this property for the stated goal.
feedbackTemplates.correctWithOptional: Correct. You also chose an optional property: {{note}}
feedbackTemplates.revealConfirm: Show the answer? This attempt will be recorded as 'answer revealed'.
feedbackTemplates.retryPrompt: Your tree is exactly as you left it. Adjust your selection and check again.

challenges.title: How many people follow this creator?

context.applicationGoal: A student portfolio website shows a creator's TikTok numbers across the top of the page. One of those numbers is the size of the creator's audience.

challenges.instruction: Select the property that holds the number of accounts following this creator.
hints: Start by scanning for values that are numbers. Then decide what each number is counting.
More than one number describes the creator's popularity. Ask whether each one counts people or counts something people did.
Rule out the number that counts reactions to videos. The one you want counts accounts.

explanation.text: The audience size is stored in `follower_count`, inside `user`, inside `data`. In this sample it is {{value:$.data.user.follower_count}}. The nearby `likes_count` ({{value:$.data.user.likes_count}}) is a different measurement: likes received across the creator's videos. The separate `error` group describes the request, not the creator; its `code` is {{value:$.error.code}} in this sample.

fieldNotes.note: An identifier TikTok can use to look up this exact request if something goes wrong.

javaRelation.summary: In a Java model this becomes a numeric field (for example a `long`) on a class that represents the creator header. The JSON path says where the value comes from; the Java field name is your own choice.

challenges.designNotes: Beginner anchor. Same container holds a sibling count with a similar name; envelope visible but collapsed to a single group.

grading.targetConcept: audience size (follower total)

rejected.feedback: That number counts the likes the creator's videos received. It measures reactions to videos, not how many accounts follow the creator.
That is text that names the creator. The goal asks for a number that counts accounts.
The error group reports how the request itself went. It holds no facts about the creator.

challenges.title: Which value could someone call?

context.applicationGoal: A travel-journal app shows a card for each bookmarked place. The card has a button that lets the student call the place.

challenges.instruction: Select the property that holds the number someone would dial to call this place.
hints: Think about what a dialable number looks like, then scan the values at the top level of the response.
Several properties are contact-style information: somewhere to go, a page to visit, a number to dial. Choose by how a person would use each one.
It is a top-level property, and its value is a string containing digits grouped like a local phone number.

explanation.text: The number to dial is `nationalPhoneNumber` ({{value:$.nationalPhoneNumber}}). It is a string, not a number, because phone numbers contain punctuation and are never used in arithmetic. `websiteUri` and `formattedAddress` are other ways to find the place, but they cannot be dialed.

fieldNotes.note: A link used to report a photo to Google; not shown on the card.

javaRelation.summary: A phone number becomes a `String` field in Java, never an `int`: leading zeros and punctuation would be lost, and you never do math on it.

challenges.designNotes: Beginner anchor with a flat top-level target; photos group stays collapsed so it acts as a plausible-but-distant distractor.

grading.targetConcept: telephone contact value

rejected.feedback: That is a web address. It is also a way to contact a place, but nobody dials it.
That tells where the place is, not how to reach it by phone.
That is a link to the photographer's page, not contact information for the place.

challenges.title: Songs in one playlist

context.applicationGoal: A playlist browser lists each of the listener's playlists with its cover picture and how many songs it holds.

challenges.instruction: Select the property that tells how many songs one playlist holds.
hints: The goal wants a count of songs, and it belongs to one playlist rather than to the whole list of playlists.
Two different numbers in this response are both tallies, but they tally different things. Check which level each one lives at.
Look inside each playlist for a small group that describes its songs, and read the number stored there.

explanation.text: A playlist's song count lives inside that playlist, in the small group named `items`, as `total`. The `total` at the very top of the response ({{value:$.total}}) counts the playlists on this page, so it answers a different question. Same name, different level, different meaning: always read a property together with the object that contains it.

fieldNotes.note: A version identifier for the playlist.

javaRelation.summary: In Java, each playlist becomes an object with its own `int`/`long` song count. The list-level count belongs to the response wrapper, not to a playlist object.

challenges.designNotes: Intermediate: identical key (total) at two levels and a nested object also called items; target is not visible until the nested object is expanded.

grading.targetConcept: song count of a single playlist

rejected.feedback: That counts the playlists in this response, not the songs inside one playlist. Check which level of the response each number belongs to.
That is the largest number of playlists this request asked for. It is a paging setting, not a fact about a playlist.
That says where in the full list this page starts. It is a paging setting, not a fact about a playlist.
That is the small group that holds the information about a playlist's songs. Open it and select the value itself, not the group.

challenges.title: Where is the AI's reply?

context.applicationGoal: A reading-practice app sends a passage to an AI model and wants to display the model's reply on screen.

challenges.instruction: Select the property that holds the words the AI wrote back.
hints: You are looking for the words the AI produced, not information about the request or about the AI itself.
The reply sits inside a list whose entries are not all the same kind. Open more than one entry and compare what each contains.
Only one list entry carries content a student would read. Inside it, look for a list of parts, then for the part that holds the words.

explanation.text: The reply words are in `text`, inside `content`, inside the second entry of `output`. The first entry has `type` {{value:$.output[0].type}} and no `content` at all, so code that blindly read position 0 would fail. `instructions` is the prompt the app sent. In this sample the string in `text` is itself JSON written as text; the app must parse it in a second step.

fieldNotes.note: How many of the input tokens were served from a cache; a billing and speed detail.

javaRelation.summary: The Java class for the reply holds a `String` for these words. Because the entries in `output` differ in kind, a robust Java model reads the entry whose `type` says it is a message rather than assuming a position.

challenges.designNotes: Intermediate: two array levels, first array entry is a different kind of item and has no content; echoed request field is a plausible trap.

grading.targetConcept: generated reply words

rejected.feedback: That is the instruction the app sent. The response repeats it for reference; it is not what the AI wrote back.
That belongs to the model's behind-the-scenes reasoning record. It is not the reply a student reads.
That reports whether the request finished. It says nothing about what was written.
That counts how large the reply was. It measures the reply but does not contain it.

challenges.title: How many times was it watched?

context.applicationGoal: A study-video gallery shows each video as a card. The card shows how popular the video is by listing how many times it has been played.

challenges.instruction: Select the property that tells how many times a video has been watched.
hints: Several properties here are counts of audience activity. List them and note what each one tallies.
One of them tallies passive watching; the others tally something a viewer actively did. Also check the data-type badges: not every count is stored the same way.
Open the group of audience measurements inside one video and choose the tally that matches the number of plays.

explanation.text: The number of plays is `viewCount`, inside `statistics`. Its value {{value:$.items[0].statistics.viewCount}} is a string even though it looks like a number: this API sends big counts as text. `likeCount`, `commentCount` and `favoriteCount` all sit beside it, but each tallies a different action. `favoriteCount` is {{value:$.items[0].statistics.favoriteCount}} here.

fieldNotes.note: A version tag the API uses for caching; not part of the video's content.

javaRelation.summary: Because this API sends the count as a JSON string, a Java model must decide how to hold it: keep it as a `String`, or convert it to a `long` after reading.

challenges.designNotes: Intermediate: four sibling counters, target stored as a string, nested one object deep inside an array element.

grading.targetConcept: play total of a video

rejected.feedback: That counts viewers who pressed like. Likes are a reaction, and far fewer than plays.
That counts written comments, which is a different kind of audience action than watching.
This counter is retired and always reads zero, so it cannot tell you how often videos were played.
That counts how many videos came back in this response, not how many times one video was watched.

relatedSamples.caption: The same request while a podcast episode is playing, for comparison.

challenges.title: Song or podcast?

context.applicationGoal: A school radio club screen shows what the DJ is playing. The DJ sometimes plays a song and sometimes a podcast episode, and the screen must choose its layout accordingly.

challenges.instruction: Select a property the screen can check to tell whether a song or a podcast episode is playing right now. Compare with the second sample before you decide.
hints: Look for a property whose value is a short label naming a category, a word rather than a number or an identifier.
Several properties carry such a label, and each describes a different thing: a device, a collection, a release, the playing item. Decide which thing the screen needs to know about.
The label you need describes what is playing itself. It may appear in more than one place; either place that describes the playing thing works.

explanation.text: Two properties answer this question. `currently_playing_type` ({{value:$.currently_playing_type}}) names the kind of thing playing, and `item.type` ({{value:$.item.type}}) carries the same label on the playing item itself. In the podcast sample both read {{value:$.currently_playing_type@s8-playback-episode}}. The other properties named `type` describe other things: the collection (`context`), the hardware (`device`), the release (`album`). A property's name alone never tells you what it describes; its parent does.

fieldNotes.note: When the player state was captured, as milliseconds since 1970 (Unix time).

javaRelation.summary: A Java model for 'now playing' usually stores this label once, as a `String` or an `enum`, and uses it to decide which fields to read next: song fields for one value, podcast fields for the other.

challenges.designNotes: Advanced: ten root keys, four plausible 'type' fields, two valid answers, and a related sample that proves the alternative. Tests equivalent-path acceptance.

grading.targetConcept: kind of the thing currently playing

accepted.label: kind of playing item
accepted.note: Also valid: the playing item carries the same label. Both are verified to match in the related podcast sample.

rejected.feedback: That describes the collection playback started from (an album or a show), not the thing playing right now.
That describes the hardware making the sound, not what is being played.
That describes the kind of release the song belongs to. A podcast episode would not even have this branch.
That is a yes/no value about playing versus paused. It does not say what is playing.

challenges.title: Distance a person can read

context.applicationGoal: A science-club board lists three possible venues. Each row shows how far the venue is from school, written the way a person would say it, unit included.

challenges.instruction: Select the property that already holds a venue's distance in a ready-to-display form.
hints: The goal wants the value a person would read on a sign, not a value a program would compute with.
Several properties describe distance or time. Some are raw numbers meant for calculation; some are pre-formatted for people.
The pre-formatted values sit in a group made for people-friendly display, and distance and time each have their own sub-group there.

explanation.text: `localizedValues` holds values the API has already formatted for people. Its `distance` entry's `text` reads {{value:$[0].localizedValues.distance.text}}. The raw `distanceMeters` ({{value:$[0].distanceMeters}}) is better for sorting or math, but the row would have to convert it and attach a unit itself. The matching `duration` pair gives time instead of distance. Note that this response is a list at the top level, so every path starts with a bare `[]`.

fieldNotes.note: Whether a route between the two places could be found.

javaRelation.summary: In Java, the display-ready distance is a `String`; the raw distance would be a number (`int` or `double`). Choose by what the screen does with the value: show it, or compute with it.

challenges.designNotes: Advanced: root-array response, three look-alike 'text' leaves under different parents, raw numeric versus display-ready distinction.

grading.targetConcept: display-ready distance

rejected.feedback: That is exact and useful for sorting, but it is a bare number in a fixed unit. The row needs a ready-to-show form that includes its unit.
That is a time, stored as a raw string in seconds. It is neither a distance nor ready to show.
That is formatted for people, but it describes travel time, not distance.
That says which destination the row refers to, not how far away it is.
That reports whether a route could be found at all. It is not a distance.

challenges.title: The friendly name

context.applicationGoal: A class app's 'What did I miss?' view shows who wrote each message. People can choose a friendly display name for themselves, but some never do.

challenges.instruction: Select the property that holds the friendly display name people choose for themselves. Remember that it can be empty for some people.
hints: Names of people can live in more than one property. Think about which one is meant for showing and which is meant for identifying.
One name-like property can be empty for some people. An empty value on one message tells you about that person, not about whether you are looking in the wrong place.
Open the group that describes the sender and compare the name-like properties across more than one message.

explanation.text: `global_name` is the friendly name. In this sample it is {{value:$[0].author.global_name}} for the first author (they never chose one) and {{value:$[2].author.global_name}} for the third. An empty (`null`) value means 'not set'; the property still exists and still is the right one. `username` is always present, which is why apps use it when the friendly name is empty.

fieldNotes.note: Bit-flag number describing special message properties; not used here.

javaRelation.summary: In Java, a value that can be missing is usually modeled so that your code checks for it (for example a `String` that may be `null`) before using it. A fallback to the handle belongs in your code's logic.

challenges.designNotes: Advanced: first element shows null for the target, so students must interpret null as 'optional', not 'wrong field'. Root-array response.

grading.targetConcept: self-chosen display name (nullable)

rejected.feedback: That is the account handle. Every account has one, so apps use it as a backup, but it is not the friendly name people choose.
That is a long identifier meant for programs. It is not meant to be read by students.
That is what the message says, not who said it.
That is a code for the sender's picture. It is not a name.
That is a legacy tag attached to the account handle. It is not a name.

challenges.title: The collection of results

context.applicationGoal: A study-video gallery builds one card for every matching video by looping over a collection.

challenges.instruction: Select the node that holds all of the matching videos together, so the loop knows what to repeat over.
hints: Look at the badges in the tree: arrays are the nodes that hold several entries that look alike.
Of the arrays and objects here, one holds entries that each look like a video. Another describes the response itself.
Select the container itself, the node with numbered children, not one of the numbered children.

explanation.text: The loop runs over `items`: an array whose numbered children are the individual videos. Selecting one numbered child (`items[0]`) picks a single video, and `pageInfo` describes the response as a whole. In a Java model this array becomes a list of video objects, one object per numbered child.

fieldNotes.note: A version tag used for caching; not part of any video.

javaRelation.summary: An array of objects in JSON usually becomes a `List` of objects in Java. The array node is the list; each numbered child is one element.

challenges.designNotes: Beginner structure anchor: array vs element vs response-level metadata. Numbered children make the array obvious.

grading.targetConcept: the repeating collection of results

rejected.feedback: That is one single video. A loop needs the whole collection that holds every video, not any one of them.
That group describes the response as a whole (how many results there are). It does not hold the videos.
That is a bookmark for asking for the next page. It is not a collection of videos.

challenges.title: About the post, or about the call?

context.applicationGoal: A club app publishes a recap video to TikTok and then reports how the post is going.

challenges.instruction: Each lettered node in the response describes either the video post or the API request itself. Choose which for every letter.
hints: For each node ask: if the call to the API failed, would this value change? If the video post failed, would it change?
Notice how the response splits into two top-level groups. Each group has its own purpose.
One group is named for problems with the call, and it describes the call even when everything went fine.

explanation.text: `data` describes the post: its `status` is {{value:$.data.status}} and `downloaded_bytes` is {{value:$.data.downloaded_bytes}}. The `error` group describes the API call itself and is present even on success; here its `code` is {{value:$.error.code}} and its `message` is empty. Seeing a group named `error` does not mean something failed.

fieldNotes.note: How many bytes of the uploaded video file TikTok has received so far.

javaRelation.summary: A Java model for this response has two parts: a small class for the post details and, separately, a place to hold the call's status and message for error handling.

challenges.designNotes: Beginner classification: two-way sort of five nodes with a useful trap (error group present on success). No arrays.

categories.label: About the video post
categories.description: Describes how the video post is progressing.

categories.label: About the API request
categories.description: Describes whether the call to the API itself worked.

grading.targetConcept: scope of each node: video post versus API request

wrong.request: This value reports how the video post is progressing, so it belongs with the post, not with the call.

wrong.post: This sits in a group about the call itself. The group exists even when the call worked, so its presence alone does not mean something went wrong.

wrong.request: This measures progress of the post's video file, so it describes the post.

wrong.post: This is a message about the call. It is empty here because the call worked.
This is an identifier for the call, useful when asking support to look something up. It says nothing about the post.

challenges.title: Opening hours, two ways

context.applicationGoal: A travel-journal card shows a place's weekly opening hours as readable lines, one for each weekday.

challenges.instruction: Fill both slots by selecting a node in the tree and then pressing its slot button.
hints: Slot 1 is a container for several related facts. Slot 2 is a list stored inside that container.
Two lists live inside the hours group: one made of small groups of numbers and one made of text a person can read. The card prints text.
Check the data-type badges on the children of the hours group. You want the array whose entries are strings.

explanation.text: `regularOpeningHours` groups everything about opening times. Inside it, `weekdayDescriptions` is an array of strings, ready to print, for example {{value:$.regularOpeningHours.weekdayDescriptions[0]}}. `periods` is an array of objects, each holding numbers like `day`, `hour` and `minute`: good for calculating whether the place is open, not for printing.

fieldNotes.note: A link for reporting a photo; not shown on the card.

javaRelation.summary: The hours group becomes a small Java class (or a nested part of one). An array of strings becomes a `List<String>`; an array of objects would need its own class for the entries.

challenges.designNotes: Beginner slot task: two related nodes in one branch, contrasting an array of strings with an array of objects.

slots.label: The group that holds all information about when the place is open
The list of ready-to-read lines, one per weekday, that the card can print

grading.targetConcept: hours group and its readable list

slots.label: The group that holds all information about when the place is open

rejected.feedback: That is one fact inside the hours group. You need the group that holds all of them.

slots.label: The list of ready-to-read lines, one per weekday, that the card can print

rejected.feedback: That is also a list, but its entries are groups of numbers (day, hour, minute) built for calculations. The card needs lines of readable text.

challenges.title: One picture, several sizes

context.applicationGoal: A video-comparison page shows a small picture for each video. The API offers each picture in several sizes, and the page picks one.

challenges.instruction: Select the node that groups all of the size options together, not a single size and not the whole description of the video.
hints: Sizes are alternatives to one another. Look for a node whose children are the same kind of thing under different labels.
It is inside the video's descriptive details, and its children are labeled with size words rather than numbered.
Do not pick one of the labeled size entries. Pick the node that contains them all.

explanation.text: `thumbnails` is an object, not an array, because its children are named options (`default`, `medium`, `high` and `standard`) instead of numbered entries. wrong.echo: The app never sent these numbers; the service reports them.

wrong.echo: The app did not send this; it describes the model that answered.
